name: White columns of the spinal cord
summary: The white matter of the cord is arranged in three funiculi on each side, each carrying a fixed set of tracts, which is what makes cord syndromes localizable in cross-section. The posterior funiculus (fasciculus gracilis and cuneatus) carries uncrossed fine touch, vibration and proprioception upward; the lateral funiculus carries the crossed lateral corticospinal tract (motor, the leg fibers lateral), the crossed spinothalamic tract (pain and temperature, sacral fibers lateral), the spinocerebellar tracts and the descending autonomic fibers; the anterior funiculus carries the anterior corticospinal, vestibulospinal and reticulospinal tracts. Lamination explains why an expanding central lesion spares sacral sensation and why extrinsic compression affects the legs first.

anatomy.location: Surrounding the gray matter: posterior funiculus between the posterior horns and the posterior median septum, lateral funiculus between the posterior and anterior horns, anterior funiculus between the anterior horn and the anterior median fissure; the anterior white commissure crosses in front of the central canal.

subdivisions.name: Posterior funiculus
subdivisions.note: fasciculus gracilis (medial, leg and lower trunk, all levels) and fasciculus cuneatus (lateral, arm and upper trunk, above T6)

subdivisions.name: Lateral funiculus
subdivisions.note: lateral corticospinal (arm medial, leg lateral), lateral spinothalamic (arm medial, sacral lateral), posterior and anterior spinocerebellar, rubrospinal, descending autonomic

subdivisions.name: Anterior funiculus
subdivisions.note: anterior corticospinal, vestibulospinal, reticulospinal, tectospinal, anterior spinothalamic, MLF

subdivisions.name: Anterior white commissure
subdivisions.note: crossing spinothalamic fibers, damaged first by a syrinx

function: Conduction of all ascending sensory and descending motor and autonomic traffic between the segments and the brain.

bestView.label: posterior, lateral and anterior funiculi around the gray matter of the upper cervical cord

imaging.normalAppearance: White matter is slightly darker than gray on axial T2 at 3 T; tract-selective signal change is diagnostic: posterior columns in B12 deficiency and copper deficiency, lateral corticospinal tracts in ALS and hereditary spastic paraplegia, anterior two-thirds in infarction.

pathology.finding: Inverted V or dumbbell T2 hyperintensity of the posterior columns in the cervical and upper thoracic cord.
Anterior two-thirds T2 hyperintensity sparing the posterior columns.
Symmetric lateral column T2 hyperintensity in ALS or adrenomyeloneuropathy.
Short peripheral wedge-shaped plaques, often dorsal or lateral.

lesionEffects.deficit: Ipsilateral loss of vibration and proprioception below the lesion
Contralateral loss of pain and temperature one to two segments below
lesionEffects.mechanism: Lateral spinothalamic tract (crossed within two segments)

lesionEffects.deficit: Ipsilateral upper motor neuron weakness below the lesion
lesionEffects.mechanism: Lateral corticospinal tract (crossed in the medulla)
Sacral spinothalamic fibers lie most laterally, away from the center

lesionEffects.deficit: Legs before arms with extrinsic compression
lesionEffects.mechanism: Leg fibers of the corticospinal tract lie laterally, nearest the surface

examination: Test each tract modality separately: vibration (posterior), pin-prick (lateral spinothalamic), power and reflexes (corticospinal)
Check perianal (sacral) sensation for sacral sparing
Compare the two sides to build a cross-sectional map
pearls: Motor and proprioceptive loss on one side with pain loss on the other is the hemicord (Brown-Séquard)
Sacral sparing means an intramedullary lesion; sacral loss first means extramedullary compression
